a b s t r a c t
Triacylglycerols (TAGs) constitute a highly efﬁcient form of energy storage. In seeds of angiosperms, they
can act as a reserve of carbon and energy allowing to fuel post-germinative seedling growth until photosynthesis becomes effective. They also constitute the economic value of seeds in many crops. In the past
years, extensive tools allowing the molecular dissection of plant metabolism have been developed
together with analytical and cytological procedures adapted for seed material. These tools have allowed
gaining a comprehensive overview of the metabolic pathways leading to TAG synthesis. They have also
unravelled factors limiting oil production such as metabolic bottlenecks and light or oxygen availability
in seed tissues. Beyond these physiological aspects, accumulation of TAGs is developmentally regulated
in seeds. The oil biosynthetic process is initiated at the onset of the maturation phase, once embryo morphogenesis is achieved. A wealth of recent studies has shed new lights on the intricate regulatory network controlling the seed maturation phase, including reserve deposition. This network involves a set
of regulated transcription factors that crosstalk with physiological signaling. The knowledge thus
acquired paves the way for the genetic engineering of oilseed crops dedicated to food applications or
green chemistry.

1. Introduction: triacylglycerols in seeds
In spermaphyta, also known as seed plants, seed development
can interrupt the life cycle and links two sporophytic generations.
This biological mechanism represents an evolutionary advantage
allowing dispersion and survival of plants, which are sessile life
forms [1]. Seeds package together all of the genetic material and
nutrients required to establish the next generation. From a genetic
point of view, seeds are chimeras originating from the fertilised
ovule. In angiosperms, the double fertilisation of the embryo sac
initiates the development of zygotic tissues, namely the diploid
embryo and the triploid endosperm (containing two maternal genome equivalents). These tissues are protected by the seed coat,
which comprises several cell layers of maternal origin derived from
the ovular integuments. Seed formation consequently requires the
coordinated growth of tissues of distinct origins and comprises two
major phases: morphogenesis and maturation. During morphogenesis, the embryo develops through a series of controlled cell divisions to progressively acquire the basic plan of the plant. The
maturation phase is characterized by (i) the accumulation of storage compounds in seed tissues, and (ii) the acquisition of dormancy and desiccation tolerance by the embryo that becomes
quiescent [2]. Whereas maturation leads to a developmental endpoint in the seed coat and endosperm, the embryo is able to germinate after a period of dormancy [1,3]. Reserve compounds stored in
the seed are then remobilized to fuel post-germinative seedling
establishment until photosynthesis becomes efﬁcient.
Seed reserve components usually consist of seed storage proteins (SSPs), carbohydrates (mostly starch), and/or storage lipids
(waxes or triacylglycerols). The relative proportion and tissue
localization of these compounds vary greatly depending on the
species considered. It is noteworthy that the carbons in fatty acids
are highly reduced, so that the oxidation of oils in germinating
seeds releases more than twice as much energy as the oxidation
of storage carbohydrates or proteins on a per g basis [4,5]. This
may explain why oils are synthesized and stored in many animal
and plant tissues, where they act as energy reserve [6]. Whereas
the desert shrub Simmondsia chinensis (jojoba) accumulates oils
in the form of liquid waxes (esters of long-chain alcohols and fatty
acids) [7], the storage lipids of seeds usually consist of triacylglycerols (TAGs).
This review focuses on the mechanisms of TAG synthesis and
accumulation. TAGs are esters of glycerol in which fatty acids are
esteriﬁed to each of the three hydroxyl groups of a glycerol backbone. Some of the fatty acids commonly found in TAGs are also
found in membrane lipids. These are predominantly palmitate
(16:0), stearate (18:0), oleate (18:1), linoleate (18:2), and a-linolenate (18:3) [8]. Nevertheless, hundreds of other fatty acids have
been described in TAGs. Substantial amounts of these ‘unususal’
fatty acid species can be deposited in the seeds of particular angiosperm families that have evolved speciﬁc fatty acid modiﬁcation
and acylation pathways [8]. For instance, oil in Brassicaceae (Brassica napus, Arabidopsis thaliana) is rich in elongated acyl chains
ranging from C20 to C24, whereas oil in other families (e.g. Lauraceae) contains shorter acyl chains ranging from C8 to C14. In castor
bean (Ricinus communis), a hydroxylated fatty acid species (ricinoleate: D9cis 18:1-OH12) is predominantly accumulated. Other families have epoxidated or methylated acyl chains in their seed oils
[5]. Whereas the fatty acid proﬁles of seed oil vary greatly from

one species to another, the analysis of 360 A. thaliana accessions
from diverse geographical locations has shown that their seeds
contain identical fatty acids, even though some variations in the
relative proportions of those fatty acid species can be observed
[9,10].
Within TAGs, fatty acids are not randomly esteriﬁed to the hydroxyl groups of the glycerol backbone. Stereochemical analyses of
the fatty acids in TAGs have shown that saturated species are usually conﬁned to the sn-1 and sn-3 positions of the glycerol, while
unsaturated species occur mainly at sn-2 [5]. In spite of the segregation of fatty acid species observed between the sn positions of
the glycerol, the variety of fatty acids present in a particular seed
oil results in the production of a heterogenous population of TAG
molecules. A limited subset of these molecular species often predominates [11–13]. Once synthesized, TAGs are stored in subcellular structures called oil bodies. These spherical organelles with a
diameter ranging from 0.2 to 2.5 lm comprise a matrix of TAGs
surrounded by a phospholipid monolayer (also called half-unit
membrane) with the aliphatic chains oriented to the TAG lumen
and the hydrophilic head groups facing the cytosol [14]. Depending
on the species considered, the abundance and location of these oil
bodies in seed tissues may vary greatly (Fig. 1). In soybean (Glycine
max), sunﬂower (Helianthus annuus), linseed (Linum usitatissimum),
safﬂower (Carthamus tinctorius), and in Brassicaceae, large
amounts of oil (and SSPs) are stored predominantly in embryo tissues (e.g. cotyledons) that occupy most of the space available in
between the integuments of the seed. The dissection of mature
seeds of the model species A. thaliana has thus shown that the
cotyledons of the embryo contain roughly 60% of total fatty acids,
radicle plus hypocotyl store 30%, and the remaining 10% are located in the residual endosperm [15,16]. In rapeseed (B. napus),
the cotyledons contain 90% of total fatty acids, with 6% in radicle
plus hypocotyl and 4% in the endosperm [15]. On the contrary, in
castor bean, oil is mostly accumulated in the large endosperm tissue that surrounds the thin embryo observed in mature seeds
[17,18]. In cereal grains, the large endosperm is the major site of
starch and SSP deposition, whereas oil accumulation is favored in
the embryo (especially in the scutellum), which usually constitutes
a small part of the seed structure [19]. Oil thus accounts for 2–3% of
seed dry weight (DW) in barley (Hordeum vulgare) or wheat (Triticum aestivum) grains [19,20]. In maize (Zea mays), the high oil content of some varieties is due to an enlarged embryo structure. Oat
(Avena sativa) is unique to cereals in that substantial amounts of oil
are stored in the endosperm of its grains (3–18% of seed DW
depending on cultivars) [21].

2. Biosynthesis and storage of triacylglycerols
The biosynthetic pathways leading to the formation of TAGs
have been widely studied in oilseeds (e.g. rapeseed or soybean).
However, in recent years, the increasing demand for plant-derived
oils and feedstock, together with the limited amount of oil crops
[22], have led to a renewed interest in the investigation of TAG synthesis into cereal grains [21]. The elucidation of oil biosynthetic
pathways has been allowed by the development and use of a wide
set of complementary techniques of plant biology ranging from
biochemistry to genetics and in vivo imaging. It is noteworthy that
a lot of these procedures have been adapted to seeds, which often

and even of the genes coding for the enzymes involved, our knowledge of the metabolic control of TAG accumulation remains partial.
This paucity of knowledge about bottlenecks or control sites has
led to very modest, or even no, changes in TAG storage in most
transgenic lines designed to modulate the expression of so-called
regulatory enzymes [24,25]. One reason for this might be that
the concept of scattered regulatory steps within the network is
partly misguided. Metabolic control analysis (MCA) experiments
have shown that control of ﬂux is often distributed throughout a
pathway. Top-down control analysis (TDCA) in particular has
established that control is exerted both by the fatty acid biosynthesis group of reactions in the plastid (referred to as Block A) and by
the complex TAG assembly group of reactions in the endoplasmic
reticulum (ER) (referred to as Block B), the relative importance of
these controls varying from one oilseed species to another
[26,27]. Within each of these blocks, metabolic control is then
shared between several enzymatic steps. Finally, it is also essential
to consider central metabolism, that provides precursors for TAG
production, and TAG storage processes to get a complete overview
of the metabolic (and cellular) processes potentially controlling oil
accumulation in seeds.

2.1. Central metabolism
Since most seeds accumulate different storage compounds in a
given cellular type, central metabolism in these cells is never entirely devoted to oil production, not even in oilseeds. In this review
however, for the sake of clarity, central metabolism is depicted as
the metabolic network linking nutrients provided by the parent
plant (sugars and amino acids) to precursors of fatty acid and
TAG synthesis, namely glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P) and acetylCoA (Fig. 2).
Sucrose represents the major form in which photosynthetically
assimilated carbon is transported into sinks such as oil accumulating seeds. Import and cleavage of this disaccharide has been shown
to play a key role in triggering the seed maturation process and
determining the strength of sink tissues in several species [28].
Whereas the sites and pathways of sucrose cleavage have been described in details in legume seeds [29], our knowledge of the
mechanisms controlling sugar unloading and cleavage in oilseeds
is limited [30]. The hexose phosphates generated by the cleavage
of sucrose can be metabolized through the glycolysis or the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway (OPPP). Theoretically, each of
these metabolic pathways can be found both in the cytosol and
in the plastids. Whereas cytosolic glycolysis is commonly accepted

as a key pathway of central metabolism in every plant cell, the
occurrence of a complete glycolytic sequence in the plastids of
oil accumulating cells has been highly debated [31,32]. Nevertheless, transcriptomic studies [33] and measurements of glycolytic
activities carried out on isolated plastids [34,35] have brought
complementary pieces of evidence strongly suggesting that the
plastidial glycolytic sequence was complete in developing embryos
of Brassicaceae species and in the endosperm of castor bean. The
status of the OPPP is quite different, since the role of the plastidial
OPPP in fatty acid production has been described in several reports
[36,37], whereas the importance of the cytosolic OPPP for the production of precursors for fatty acid biosynthesis remains unclear
[38]. Two glycolytic intermediates are utilized as precursors for
TAG synthesis. First, the conversion of cytosolic dihydroxyacetone
phosphate (DHAP) to G3P by G3P dehydrogenases (G3PDH) provides the glycerol backbones necessary for the synthesis of TAG
molecules. The availability of G3P was proposed to restrict the

overall rate of TAG accumulation [39]. In agreement with this, a
transgenic approach relying on the seed-speciﬁc expression of a
yeast gene coding for cytosolic G3PDH in oilseed rape has led to
a three- to fourfold increase in the level of G3P in developing seeds,
resulting in a 40% increase in the ﬁnal seed oil content [40]. Then,
the oxidative decarboxylation of plastidial pyruvate by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) produces CO2 and acetyl-CoA
[41–43], the latter being used as a precursor for de novo fatty acid
synthesis in the plastids.
Beyond the complex network deﬁned by interconnected OPPPs
and glycolytic pathways, additional metabolic routes can participate in supplying precursors for de novo fatty acid synthesis. In
green photoheterotrophic plastids of B. napus embryos, ribulose1,5-bisphophate carboxylase/oxygenase (RuBisCO) is able to ﬁx
CO2 apart from the Calvin cycle and to operate as part of a recently
identiﬁed metabolic route. This RuBisCO shunt involves the conversion of hexose phosphates to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate

(Ru1,5P) by the non-oxidative reactions of the OPPP together with
phosphoribulokinase (PRK), and the subsequent conversion of
Ru1,5P and CO2 to 3-phosphoglycerate (3PGA) by RuBisCO [44]
(Fig. 2). Phosphoglycerate can be further metabolized to pyruvate
and thence to fatty acids via acetyl-CoA. This metabolic route offsets the loss of CO2 at reactions such as the pyruvate dehydrogenase, thus increasing the efﬁciency of carbon use in maturing
embryos. Another route for the synthesis of plastidial pyruvate
(and thence acetyl-CoA) is through decarboxylation of imported
malate by the plastidial NADP-dependent malic enzyme (ME)
[45,46]. Supply of malate relies on either the translocation of mitochondrial malate or the reﬁxation of CO2 into oxaloacetate (OAA)
by cytosolic phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC), followed
by the conversion of OAA into malate catalyzed by NAD-dependent
malate dehydrogenase (MDH) [47–50]. Additional routes for the
synthesis of acetyl-CoA in the plastids of oilseed have been proposed that were through plastidial acetyl-CoA synthetase [51], carnitine acyltransferase, or ATP-citrate lyase (ACL) [31]. However, the
proposed mechanisms are highly controversial and the corresponding pathways, when existing, may not represent major
routes to de novo fatty acid synthesis [52].
Considering both the complexity and partial redundancy of
metabolic pathways leading to the production of precursors for
de novo fatty acid synthesis, decades of research have addressed
the relative proportion of carbon ﬂuxes through these pathways.
A wide set of investigations has ﬁrstly relied on the isolation of intact plastids and the study of their ability to incorporate exogenously supplied metabolites into fatty acid products [31].
However, recent data suggest that isolated plastids do not quantitatively reﬂect the ﬂuxes occurring in vivo [36]. The combination of
transcriptomic and proteomic approaches coupled to the use of
high throughput metabolite and enzyme assays in either wild-type
or mutant developing seeds have then provided valuable data for
the elucidation of carbon metabolism in oilseeds. More recently,
13
C metabolic ﬂux analysis (13C MFA) has been adapted to developing embryos and has considerably increased our understanding of
metabolic ﬂuxes in this material [53–55]. Nevertheless, one limitation to this powerful technique is that embryos are cultured
in vitro, and potential effects of culture conditions on developing
embryos must be considered, as the ﬁndings of MFA might not represent exactly the ﬂuxes occurring in planta [36]. Considering the
set of data available to date, it appears that metabolic ﬂuxes vary
from one oilseed species to another. In Brassicaceae such as B. napus or A. thaliana, green photoheterototrophic embryos import sucrose. A major route for carbon may involve the cytosolic glycolytic
pathway up to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), this compound being
imported into the plastid before subsequent conversion to pyruvate, then to acetyl-CoA; the essentially irreversible transphosphorylation from PEP to pyruvate is catalyzed by plastidial pyruvate
kinase [56,57], the subsequent oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to produce acetyl-CoA and CO2 is catalyzed by the PDC [58].
Another part of the carbon for fatty acid synthesis is provided by
3-PGA derived from the RuBisCO [59]. In non-green heterotrophic
embryos of sunﬂower, most carbon from the cytosol enters the
plastids at the level of hexoses. Net forward ﬂux through the upper
part of glycolysis appears to be conﬁned to the plastid, whereas the
subcellular location of the lower part of glycolysis has not been
determined so far. A signiﬁcant plastidial OPPP activity also participates to the conversion of hexoses into triose-phosphates. Finally,
a minor part (less than 10%) of the carbon for fatty acid synthesis is
attributable to the import of malate and the subsequent conversion
of this compound in pyruvate by NADP-dependent ME [36].
In depth analysis of mitochondrial metabolism in embryos of
oilseeds has been carried out thanks to the development and use
of tools dedicated to the evaluation of metabolic ﬂuxes. In species
studied so far (rapeseed, soybean, sunﬂower) import of pyruvate

from the cytosol and its subsequent decarboxylation by the mitochondrial PDC represents an important source of carbon for the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. Fluxes through anaplerotic enzymes
contribute little to feed the TCA cycle with OAA. Amino acid import
from the parent plant is also proposed to participate to the replenishment of intermediates of the TCA cycle. In rapeseed or sunﬂower for instance, imported Gln may be converted to Glu by a
cytosolic glutamate synthase; a mitochondrial glutamate dehydrogenase may then use Glu to replenish a-ketoglutarate (KG) [36,59].

appears to be preferred over succinate thiokinase reaction [60,61].

repression of mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase stimulates oil accumulation in seeds [63,64]. The authors suggested
that the mitochondrial acetyl-CoA over-accumulated in these

2.2. Fatty acid synthesis
De novo synthesis of fatty acids occurs in the plastids and acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) is considered to catalyze the ﬁrst committed step of the pathway (Fig. 3) [66,67]. The formation of
malonyl-CoA from acetyl-CoA and bicarbonate by ACC has long
been considered as a key regulatory step of the fatty acid biosynthetic process. Consequently, the mechanism of this two-step reaction, which requires biotin as a cofactor, has been extensively
studied [68]. In plastids of dicots and non-Poacae monocots, ACC
consists of four separate subunits assembled into a 700-kD complex, referred to as prokaryotic or heteromeric (HtACC) [69]. In
plastids of Poacae, ACC consists in a single large multifunctional
polypeptide; the structure is termed eukaryotic or homomeric
(HmACC) and is also found in the cytosol of all plant species
[70,71]. The overexpression of a HmACC targeted to the plastids
of transgenic B. napus was reported to stimulate fatty acid accumulation in seeds, possibly because the homomeric isoform used was
escaping negative feedback regulations exerted over the heteromeric isoform usually found in the plastids of this species [72].
On the contrary, the seed-speciﬁc overexpression of BCCP2 (encoding the biotin binding subunit of plastidial HtACC) in A. thaliana
produced lower seed oil compared with nontransgenic lines [73].
The phenotype was attributed to the production of non-biotinylated HtACC complexes altering seed metabolism [74] and illustrates
the importance of a balanced production of both protein components of HtACC and biotin cofactor for an efﬁcient fatty acid
production.
The malonyl-CoA produced by plastidial ACC constitutes the
carbon donor for each cycle of the fatty acid biosynthetic pathway.
Before entering the biosynthetic process, the malonyl group is
transferred from CoA to a protein cofactor named acyl carrier protein (ACP) by a malonyl-CoA:acyl carrier protein S-malonytransferase (MAT) [75–77]. Fatty acids are produced by an easily
dissociable multisubunit complex consisting of monofunctional
enzymes and referred to as fatty acid synthase (FAS) [67,78]. FAS
uses acetyl-CoA as a starting unit and malonyl-ACP as the
elongator (Fig. 3). The malonyl-thioester enters into a series of

2.3. Triacylglycerol assembly
TAG assembly takes place in the ER and utilizes G3P and acylCoAs as primary substrates (Fig. 3). Multiple interconnected pathways leading to TAG biosynthesis have been described in maturing
oilseeds [106]. Acyl-CoAs, as provided directly from de novo fatty
acid synthesis and from other sources, are used for the sequential
sn-1 and sn-2 acylations of G3P. The ﬁrst acylation reaction is catalyzed by a glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase (GPAT) and
yields lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), which in turn is acylated by a
lysophosphatidic acid acyltransferase (LPAAT) to produce the central metabolite phosphatidic acid (PA). PA is then converted to 1,2sn-diacylglycerol (DAG) by the action of PA phosphatase (PAP). In
the straightforward Kennedy pathway [107], a third fatty acid is
transferred to the vacant position sn-3 of DAG by 1,2-sn-diacylglycerol acyltransferase (DGAT), the only enzymatic reaction of the
pathway exclusively committed to TAG biosynthesis [108,109]. Beyond the two families of membrane-bound DGATs characterized so
far, namely DGAT1 and DGAT2, a soluble DGAT has been recently
characterized in peanut (Arachis hypogeal) cotyledons [110]. In
the same line, a novel class of acyl-CoA-dependent acyltransferases, wax ester synthase/diacylglycerol acyltransferase (WS/DGAT)
has recently been described, but its involvement in seed oil biosynthesis remains to be established [111]. Several biotechnological approaches relying on the overexpression of cDNAs encoding
acyltransferases of the Kennedy pathway have been reported.
Transgenic plants over-expressing GPATs [112] or LPAATs
[113,114] exhibit contrasting enrichments in seed oil content. A
number of studies have then suggested that DGAT may catalyze
the rate-limiting reaction in TAG bioassembly [39,115–117]. The
mounting evidence for the possible regulatory role of DGAT in
determining seed oil content [118] has led to numerous attempts
aimed at increasing this oil content by over-expressing either naturally occurring DGATs or mutagenized versions of the enzyme
during seed maturation [119]. Results obtained vary greatly
depending on the cDNA utilized, the species transformed, and
the growth conditions considered [65]. Whereas GPATs do not exhibit strong substrate speciﬁcity in vivo, LPAATs and DGATs exhibit
stringent substrate speciﬁcity and this has to be taken into account
in the design of biotechnological strategies aimed at accumulating
unusual fatty acids in seeds.
DAG represents an important branch point between non-polar
and membrane lipid biosynthesis, and fatty acids produced in the
plastids are not always immediately available for TAG biosynthesis
[106]. Instead, DAG may be converted to PC by CDP-choline:1,2-sndiacylglycerol cholinephosphotransferase (CPT), and acyl residues
are then further desaturated by fatty acid desaturases or otherwise
modiﬁed by FAD2-like enzymes (see above). There are several possible routes whereby acyl residues from PC can be incorporated
into TAG. First, the CPT reaction being rapidly reversible [120],
the DAG moiety of PC can be liberated by hydrolysis, thus becoming available for TAG ﬁnal bioassembly by DGAT. Recently, a phosphatidylcholine:1,2-sn-diacylglycerol choline phosphotransferase
(PDCT) was characterized that interconverts DAG and PC during
TAG synthesis and provides a major route for desaturated acyl
chains to be returned to the DAG pool [121]. Acyl chains from PC
may then become available for TAG biosynthesis by acyl exchange
between a fatty acid attached to CoA (from the acyl-CoA pool) and

2.4. Storage of triacylglycerols
Once TAG bioassembly is achieved in the ER, possibly in specialized sub-domains of the organelle [123], TAGs are transferred and
accumulated into subcellular structures called oil bodies or oleosomes. These spherical organelles with a diameter ranging from
0.2 to 2.5 lm depending on the species comprise a matrix of TAGs
surrounded by a phospholipid monolayer where the aliphatic
chains are oriented to the TAG lumen and the phosphate groups toward the cytosol [124]. Oil bodies probably arise from microdomains of the ER. However, the mechanism of their biogenesis is
highly debated [125–127]. A speciﬁc subset of proteins is embedded in the lipid monolayer of oil bodies that represents 1–4% of
the weight of these organelles [128–130]. This proteome has been
described in an exhaustive manner in several Brassicaceae species
[131–133]. Oleosins are the most abundant proteins found in these
proteomes. They may cover the entire surface of oleosomes,
improving the stability of the organelle by means of steric hindrance and electronegative repulsion, so that compressed oil
bodies never coalesce or aggregate in the cells of mature seeds
[125,134,135]. In addition to oleosins, other proteins like caleosins,
steroleosins, and aquaporins have been isolated in the lipid monolayer of oil bodies. Some of these proteins, together with oleosins,

play critical roles during the degradation of storage lipids through
ß-oxidation after germination [136].
Some seed tissues accumulate TAGs that are not remobilized
after germination. This is the case of the endosperm of monocot
grains, that undergoes programmed cell death during the maturation phase [137] and thus has no capacity for ß-oxidation after germination. Intriguingly, oil body fusions have been described in this
tissue to such an extent that oil appears as a smear throughout the
cells of endosperm in mature oat grains [138]; this might be the
consequence of a lack of oleosins. Such a phenomenon has already
been described in the mesocarp of olive (Olea europaea) fruits: the
oil stored in this tissue is not used as an energy store for the plant
but as an attractant for fruit predators, which thereby disperse the
seeds [139].
3. Physiological control of seed oil production
3.1. Energy requirements for fatty acid biosynthesis
The high reduction level of carbons in fatty acids explains why
the oxidation of oils releases much more energy than the oxidation
of carbohydrates or proteins. Accordingly, fatty acid synthesis has a
higher demand for energy and depends upon the stromal provision
of ATP and reducing equivalents (Fig. 4) [140]. De novo fatty acid
synthesis requires stoichiometric amounts of ATP, NADPH, and
NADH for each sequential addition of an acetyl unit to the growing
chain of the fatty acid. ATP is required for the carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA by ACC, whereas the two reductases of the
FAS complex, namely KAR and ENR, require NADPH and NADH,
respectively. Plastids of oilseeds must either take up ATP and
reductant or generate them internally. Import of reducing equivalents or ATP generated in the mitochondria or cytosol requires specialized transporters such as ATP/ADP exchange translocators that
have been poorly investigated in oilseeds [31]. A potential source
for ATP and reductant within the plastids is that generated by

3.2. Oxygen as a limiting factor
Oxygen depletion appears to be a common feature of plant tissues with low surface area to volume ratio such as organs dedicated to the accumulation of storage compounds, including
oilseeds [144–146]. In seeds, this phenomenon is emphasized by
the low permeability of maternal tissues (e.g. silique/pod walls
and seed integuments) for gases. In seeds of B. napus grown at
ambient external oxygen (21%) in the light, oxygen falls to 17% in
the internal silique space and 0.8% within seeds [145]. This low
oxygen tension may be accompanied by a reduction in the ATP/
ADP ratios and a subsequent limitation of biosynthetic ﬂuxes in
maturing oilseeds. Accordingly, an inhibition of seed storage compound accumulation was reported when plants are grown at low
(subambient) external oxygen whereas superambiant oxygen concentrations stimulate the rate of TAG synthesis [145,147]. Despite
low oxygen levels and impaired respiration, embryonic metabolism is highly controlled, adjusting metabolic ﬂuxes to prevent anoxia and limit fermentation. A switch to pathways that consume
less ATP and utilize oxygen more efﬁciently constitutes an efﬁcient
response to low-oxygen conditions. This may be achieved by the
activation of PPi-dependent metabolic pathways and bypasses: in
maturing seeds of A. thaliana, the activation of the PPi-consuming
sucrose synthase pathway together with a switch from ATP-dependent phosphofructokinase to a PPi-dependent phosphofructokinase activities were observed during seed maturation [148,149].
By recycling waste energy to fuel important central metabolic
functions under low oxygen, PPi-associated pathways may contribute to avoid anoxia in the maturing embryo. However, the importance of PPi metabolism in oilseeds remains to be ﬁrmly
established [150]. Restriction of oil metabolism constitutes another
part of the adaptive response to low oxygen concentrations [145].
Whereas oxygen availability clearly limits TAG biosynthesis under
certain growth conditions, starch storage metabolism seems to be
less affected. This has led to hypothesize a general role of oxygen
on the lipid/starch balance during oilseed development in Brassicaceae [151,152]. Likewise, the in vivo oxygen distribution in maize
kernels favors assimilate partitioning toward starch within O2-depleted regions of endosperm while TAGs are stored in well-oxygenated regions at the kernel periphery, in embryo, aleurone, and
vitreous layers of endosperm [153].
3.3. Importance of light and contribution of embryo photosynthesis to
energy metabolism
Whereas plastids isolated from maturing seeds of castor bean,
safﬂower, and sunﬂower are chlorophyll-less, several oilseeds like
soybean, linseed, and rapeseed are green and utilize photosynthe-

243

sis to drive oil biosynthetic processes. Because the transmittance of
light through the silique/pod wall and seed integuments is fairly
low [154,48,155], the pigment composition of green embryos reﬂects shade adaptation, with a Chl a/b ratio lower than in leaves
[156]. Although green oilseeds contain chloroplasts with the thylakoid structures and enzymes of typical photosynthetic machinery,
these seeds remain predominantly sink tissues. They operate a
mixed economy, with the capacity to simultaneously utilize autotrophic and heterotrophic pathways of energy production to sustain anabolic reactions [142]. The behaviour of their chloroplasts
is termed photoheterotrophism. Light conditions during oilseed
maturation have been shown to strongly inﬂuence oil yield in soybean, rapeseed, and A. thaliana, with seeds from higher light tending to exhibit increased oil content [15,156,157]. Light stimulates
oil accumulation through photosynthesis at several levels.
First, light reactions produce ATP and NADPH that can be used
for energetically expansive fatty acid synthesis in the plastids
[158]. In green seeds like in leaves, the balance between cyclic
and non-cyclic photophosphorylation may adjust respective ATP
and NADPH productions to metabolic requirements [159]. It is
noteworthy that the capacity of oilseeds to harness light is inversely related to the importance of the TCA cycle in providing ATP.
In chlorophyll-less sunﬂower embryos, ﬂux through citrate synthase represents 85% of glucose uptake and mitochondrial respiration accounts for 100% of biosynthetic ATP demand [36]. On the
contrary, in green embryos of B. napus, ﬂux around the TCA cycle
is absent and the small ﬂuxes through oxidative reactions in the
mitochondria can generate at most 22% of biosynthetic ATP demand [59].
Second, photosynthetic oxygen release can play a key role in the
local energy state by maintaining the respiratory ATP production
and preventing anoxia, so that oilseed metabolism is not restricted
[155]. The sites of photosynthetic oxygen release and consumption
can be distinct: in maturing soybean seeds for instance, an inverse
relationship between photosynthesis (located in the abaxial region
or outer part of the cotyledons) and TAG biosynthesis (localized in
the adaxial region or inner part of the cotyledons) was observed
that unravelled the diffusion of photosynthetic oxygen toward
the embryo interior where it promotes respiration, followed by local increases in the energy state [160].
Third, activation of the RuBisCO bypass (Fig. 2) increases the
efﬁciency of carbon use during the formation of oil, offsetting the
loss of CO2 at the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction in particular
[44]. Chlorophyll-less sunﬂower embryos thus convert carbon supplies into reserves with an average efﬁciency of 50% that contrasts
with the efﬁciency of over 80% observed for the green embryos of
B. napus [36,157]. If green oilseeds maximise oil synthesis during
light periods, those syntheses appear to be drastically reduced during the night [156]. Lowering the rate of oil production during the
night may be a strategy to reduce carbon lost as CO2. This diurnal
carbon conservation strategy may ultimately lead to more oil storage in seeds [157].

storage lipids in plants grown at lower temperatures are generally
enriched in polyunsaturated fatty acids, the extent of unsaturation
being inversely related to the temperature [162,163]. The inﬂuence
of the temperature on the proportion of unsaturated fatty acids is
weak in safﬂower seeds [164], moderate in soybean and rapeseed
[163,165], and high in sunﬂower [166,167]. Several mechanisms

4. Developmental control of triacylglycerol accumulation
4.1. Activation of the maturation program in seeds
Oil accumulation is part of the seed maturation process, a
highly controlled developmental program that sets in embryo tissues once morphogenesis is achieved. The maturation process is

characterized by storage compound accumulation, acquisition of
desiccation tolerance, and entry into a dormancy period of variable
length. Gene expression programs related to these processes are
activated during the maturation phase and switched off during
vegetative phases of plant development. Accordingly, studies carried out on developing seeds and/or embryos have established that
the biosynthetic pathways for fatty acids and TAGs are regulated at
the level of transcription [149,175,176] (Fig. 5). In A. thaliana,
microarray analyses have revealed differential timing of the activation of genes involved in storage lipid metabolism during seed
maturation [177]. Genes encoding fatty acid synthesis enzymes
display a bell-shaped pattern of expression at the onset of the maturation phase, whereas the expression level of several fatty-acid
modifying enzymes and oleosins increases later [178].
Genetic studies in maize and A. thaliana have delineated a complex network of transcription factors that control the gene expression programs essential to accomplish seed maturation. A wide set
of activators and repressors were thus shown to control the
transition between vegetative phases of development and seed
maturation [179]. Chromatin remodeling events together with
transcriptional regulations trigger the activity of the activators of
the maturation program in developing seeds, whereas the activity
of repressors becomes preponderant in late maturing and germinating seeds, and in vegetative organs of the plant [180,181].
Loss-of-function mutations affecting the activators of the seed
maturation program usually leads to bypass of the maturation
phase, including severe defects in oil storage [182]. Conversely, ectopic expression of these activators confers embryonic characteristics to transgenic seedlings, triggering TAG accumulation in
rosettes leaves for instance [183–185]. Loss-of-function mutations
affecting the repressors of the maturation program also confers
embryonic characteristics to seedlings that accumulate TAGs
[186,187], and it is tempting to speculate that a seed-speciﬁc overexpression of these actors would inhibit TAG storage and other

4.2. Direct regulation of the fatty acid biosynthetic pathway
Transcripts of genes encoding plastidial enzymes of the late glycolysis and fatty acid biosynthetic pathway accumulate in a coordinated manner during seed maturation [176]. This observation
suggests that these genes might be co-regulated. Whereas fatty
acid biosynthetic genes strongly respond to variations/perturbations of the expression level of activators and repressors of the
maturation program, they are not direct targets of the master regulators of seed maturation. The isolation of an A. thaliana mutant
speciﬁcally impaired in TAG accumulation in seeds, namely wrinkled1 (wri1) [208], has allowed building a model that reconciles
these apparently divergent observations [178]. WRI1 encodes a
transcription factor of the APETALA2-ethylene responsive element-binding protein (AP2-EREBP) family [209] that speciﬁes the
regulatory action of LEC2 and possibly LEC1 toward the fatty acid
biosynthetic network [210]. This regulatory cascade allows ﬁnetuning the expression of seed-induced, though not seed-speciﬁc,
fatty acid biosynthetic genes. WRI1 interacts with the promoter sequences of PKp-ß1, BCCP2, and KAS1 in vitro and/or in yeast one-hybrid experiments [211,212]. An AW-box sequence [CnTnG(n)7CG]
identiﬁed in the promoter regions of several glycolytic and fatty
acid biosynthetic genes was proposed to be recognized by WRI1
[211]; nevertheless, a 15-bp element [cAAAAG(t/g)Agg(g/a)gttT]

was also identiﬁed that plays a key role in the activation of these
genes [212]. Further investigations are required to fully understand
the transcriptional mechanisms controlling fatty acid biosynthesis
in seeds. Considering that the transcript accumulation of target
genes of WRI1 is not completely abolished in wri1 null mutants,
it is tempting to speculate that one or several elements of the transcriptional machinery remain to be identiﬁed.

5. Conclusion: toward a biotechnological control of
triacylglycerol accumulation
TAGs produced by domesticated oilseed crops are used primarily for nutritional applications. In recent years however, there has
been increasing demand for production of biofuels and chemical
feedstocks [213]. The fatty acyl chains are chemically similar to
the aliphatic hydrocarbons found in petroleum [22]. In light of rising petroleum prices and environmental concerns, the use of plant
oils as renewable sources of fuel and industrial raw material has
consequently been considered with renewed interest. In the near
future, the production of industrially important oils in oilseed
crops engineered through plant biotechnology approaches may
represent a key step in the transition from a fossil oil-based society
to a sustainable, bio-based economy [214]. For this purpose, the
knowledge acquired in the recent years about the physiological
and developmental regulation of seed oil production will prove
particularly useful. However, more research will be required to
fully decipher the structural and regulatory aspects of oil biosynthesis that have important implications with regard to the possibilities for creating transgenic plant with desired oil qualities [213].
Several excellent reviews have recently described in detail the
numerous attempts that have been made to genetically engineer
oilseeds to produce nutritional or industrial fatty acids [215–
219]. If many of these efforts have met with only modest success,
accumulation of some target fatty acids has been remarkably successful. For instance, transgenic expression in rapeseed of a laurate
speciﬁc acyl-ACP thioesterase from the California bay tree
(Umbellularia californica) together with a laurate-speciﬁc LPAAT
from coconut has led to the accumulation of up to 67% laurate in
the seed TAG [220]. In the same line, when transgenic rapeseed
lines expressing a LPAAT gene from Limnanthes alba and an extra
copy of the rapessed FAE1 elongase gene were crossed with a rape
variety with high oleic acid content, individual seeds with over 70%
erucic acid were obtained [214]. Recent strides in plant molecular
biology have even allowed the introduction of complex multigene
biosynthetic pathways such as the one synthesizing omega-3 longchain polyunsaturated fatty acids [221,222]. However, none of the
corresponding crops have been commercialized so far.
If some of the efforts devoted to produce industrial fatty acids in
transgenic plants are encouraging, the conversion of plant oils to
biodiesel and chemical feedstocks competes with their use as food.
To ensure that these new industrial productions do not affect the
supply of food at a time when food requirements are steeply
increasing worldwide, seed oil production has to be dramatically
increased, ideally with minimal environmental impact [22]. Proposals such as the use of drought-resistant oilseed plants capable
of growing on non-arable wasteland (Jatropha curcas) or the production of TAGs by algae or yeast have been put forward
[223,224]. Alternatively, increasing seed oil content, and thence
the yield of oil per unit area of arable land constitutes another paramount of importance in supplying enough oil for food and nonfood applications [65]. So far, contributions to enhancing seed oil
content have come about mainly through conventional breeding
[65]. In the near future, further improvements of seed oil content
in crop species may arise from genetic engineering aimed at controlling the ﬂow of carbon into seed oil. To increase efﬁciently seed
